chunks: "A core is a piece of magnetic material, like ferrite or powdered iron, that the winding goes around. Its job is to guide and concentrate the magnetic flux.
Inductance depends on the number of turns squared divided by the reluctance of the flux path.
Air has a very high reluctance, but a core with a relative permeability of hundreds or thousands has a much lower one, so the same number of turns gives far more inductance.
A ferrite toroid with permeability 2000 gives 2000 times the inductance of the same winding in air. That means smaller inductors and fewer turns, so less copper loss.
The core also confines the field, so it reduces coupling to nearby circuits, and it lets multiple windings share the same flux, which is how transformers and coupled inductors work.
The costs: a core can only carry so much flux before it saturates, and then the inductance collapses.
It also has losses from the changing flux, hysteresis and eddy currents, which heat it and limit the frequency range. Permeability changes with temperature, frequency and bias.
For power inductors, we often put an air gap in the core.
The gap has a high reluctance, so it reduces the inductance but stores the energy and lets the inductor carry much more DC current before saturating.
In one example, a one millimeter gap drops the inductance from 1. 1 millihenries to 54 microhenries but raises the saturation current from 0. 4 to 8. 4 amps."
